Here is the story of a remarkable, independent treatment suggestion by GPT-5 Pro: repurposing a known drug for a patient with food protein–induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES).

First, how we came to test this. My close friend, physician-scientist Dr. Oral Alpan, treated the patient described in the published report (link in the thread) for refractory allergic skin disease with the biologic dupilumab, which is approved for that indication. The patient also had FPIES, a food allergy that in his case was triggered by wheat and caused hours of cramping and watery, sometimes bloody, diarrhea. There is no approved treatment for FPIES; patients are advised to avoid trigger foods and prepare for emergencies if accidental exposure occurs. For twenty years, even a small amount of wheat set off the same cascade a few hours later, followed by days of recovery.

After starting dupilumab for his skin condition, the patient traveled to France and accidentally ate a baguette. To his surprise, nothing happened! It was his first uneventful wheat exposure in two decades! On return, Dr. Alpan hypothesized that dupilumab might be responsible and supervised an oral food challenge approaching 50 grams of wheat protein. Again, no reaction! When an insurance interruption forced a pause in medication, the old symptoms returned; restarting it restored tolerance. In the peer-reviewed paper published today, Dr. Alpan and his team describe seven additional patients, ages 2 to 58, who responded to dupilumab for their FPIES condition. 

While this is not definitive proof and represents an observational case series, the findings suggest that dupilumab could be a potential treatment for FPIES. Dr. Alpan intends to contact Regeneron, the manufacturer, to pursue clinical studies hopefully toward FDA approval for this disease.

About two months ago, as he had just submitted the paper on this case, Dr. Alpan told me this story. Until today’s publication there were no reports in the literature of dupilumab potentially treating FPIES. Around that time GPT-5 Pro had just been released, and I thought this would be a perfect case to test whether AI could infer a treatment from the clinical case alone. MITが、AIの歴史を塗り替える新技術「Tensor Logic」を紹介する論文を発表しました。 

「Tensor Logic」は、論理的推論を純粋な数学（テンソル代数）に変換し、AIにおける「学習」と「論理」の長年の対立に終止符を打ちます。

つまり、ニューラルネットワークが論理的に思考し、論理システムがデータから学習する、真の統合が実現します。

この衝撃的な論文を6つのポイントにまとめました。

1. 「論理」を「数学」へ変換
Tensor Logicは、論理的な命題を「ベクトル」に、推論ルールを「テンソル演算」に変換します。記号操作や探索に頼るのではなく、すべてが微分可能な数学的処理として実行されるため、ニューラルネットワークと論理推論が初めて「同じ言語」を話せるようになります。

2. AIの根本的な問題を解決
これまでのAIは、「True/False」のような離散的な論理と、ニューラルネットが得意な連続的な勾配計算が相容れませんでした。Tensor Logicは、ブール論理や述語論理さえも単一の微分可能なフレームワークに埋め込むことで、この根本的な壁を打ち破ります。

3. 論理的保証を持つ学習
これにより、ニューラルネットワークのようにエンドツーエンドでシステム全体を学習させながら、数学的な論理の正確性を保証することが可能になります。AIが単に「それらしい答え」を出すのではなく、「証明可能な答え」を導き出せるようになります。

4. 驚異的な計算効率と拡張性
複雑な論理クエリも、GPUが得意な行列演算の速度で処理できます。これにより、従来の記号AIが直面していた「組み合わせ爆発」と呼ばれる計算量の問題を回避し、大規模な問題にも対応できるスケーラビリティを実現します。

5. ハルシネーションの克服
Tensor Logicは、従来のAIが抱えていた2つの大きな弱点を克服します。記号AIの曖昧さと、ニューラルネットワークが犯す「論理的なハルシネーション（もっともらしい嘘）」です。AIが現実世界の曖昧なデータから、数学的な確実性をもって推論する道が開かれます。

6. 社会実装への巨大なインパクト
この技術は、自動運転、医療診断、金融システム、法務など、高い信頼性と論理的正確性が求められるあらゆる分野に革命をもたらす可能性があります。「学習が得意」か「論理が得意」か、どちらか一方しかなかったAIの時代は、終わりを告げました。

Forget Individual Genius—The Future of AI Is All About Family Trees

(1/10)

The secret to building a superintelligent AI isn't to reward genius.

It's to reward good parenting.

A new paper just dropped that completely changes how we think about AI self-improvement, and it's a wild ride.
🧵

(2/10)

For years, the logic for making AI smarter seemed simple:

Test an AI on a task (like coding).
If it gets a high score, let it "evolve" its own code.
Repeat.

But new research shows this is a TRAP. They call it the "Metaproductivity-Performance Mismatch."

I call it the "Sterile Genius Problem."

(3/10)

The "Sterile Genius" is an AI that gets a high score but its self-modifications lead to evolutionary dead ends. It's a one-hit-wonder.

Meanwhile, a lower-scoring AI might be a "Great Ancestor," seeding a whole dynasty of future AIs that achieve incredible things.

So, how do you find the great ancestors and ignore the sterile geniuses?

(4/10)
Enter the Huxley-Gödel Machine (HGM).

Instead of looking at an AI's individual score, it looks at its entire "clade"—its family tree of descendants.

It stops asking: "How smart is this AI?"

And starts asking: "Does this AI produce successful kids?"

(5/10)

Think of it like this:

Don't reward the one-hit-wonder musician who wrote one catchy song.

Reward the music teacher whose students consistently top the charts for decades.

HGM is a system designed to find and promote the best AI teachers, not just the best performers.

(6/10)

And the name? It's just as cool as the idea.

Huxley: For the evolutionary biologist who championed the idea of 'clades' (lineages).

Gödel: For the Gödel Machine, a theoretical "optimally self-improving" AI.

HGM is a practical way to approximate that optimal, god-tier self-improvement. 

(7/10)

And it works. The researchers pitted HGM against older methods.

Not only did HGM discover better coding agents, but it did so with staggering efficiency, using 2x to 6x FEWER allocated CPU-hours.

It's smarter at finding talent and more efficient.

But that's not even the most interesting part.

An agent discovered by HGM (using a smaller model) was given a more powerful "brain" (GPT-5) and tested on a new benchmark.

The result? It achieved performance on par with the BEST human-engineered AI agents on the official leaderboard.

It didn't just learn to code. It evolved a superior design for itself.

This gives us a new lens for the future.
Next time you see an AI break a record, ask yourself:
"Is it a sterile genius, or the start of a dynasty?"

The answer tells you everything about its true potential for growth. This is the question that will define the next decade of AI.

(10/10)

Because this research suggests the future of AI won't be built by a single, perfect genius.

It will be raised by a great ancestor.

First, how we came to test this. My close friend, physician-scientist Dr. Oral Alpan, treated the patient described in the published report (link in the thread) for refractory allergic skin disease with the biologic dupilumab, which is approved for that indication. The patient also had FPIES, a food allergy that in his case was triggered by wheat and caused hours of cramping and watery, sometimes bloody, diarrhea. There is no approved treatment for FPIES; patients are advised to avoid trigger foods and prepare for emergencies if accidental exposure occurs. For twenty years, even a small amount of wheat set off the same cascade a few hours later, followed by days of recovery.

After starting dupilumab for his skin condition, the patient traveled to France and accidentally ate a baguette. To his surprise, nothing happened! It was his first uneventful wheat exposure in two decades! On return, Dr. Alpan hypothesized that dupilumab might be responsible and supervised an oral food challenge approaching 50 grams of wheat protein. Again, no reaction! When an insurance interruption forced a pause in medication, the old symptoms returned; restarting it restored tolerance. In the peer-reviewed paper published today, Dr. Alpan and his team describe seven additional patients, ages 2 to 58, who responded to dupilumab for their FPIES condition. 

While this is not definitive proof and represents an observational case series, the findings suggest that dupilumab could be a potential treatment for FPIES. Dr. Alpan intends to contact Regeneron, the manufacturer, to pursue clinical studies hopefully toward FDA approval for this disease.

There were several other suggestions, though those are most obvious ones and also suggested by other models too. This paper builds an agentic LLM that can run the whole data science workflow by itself.

It is an 8B model that plans work, reads structured files, writes and runs code, checks results, and iterates. 

Standard “workflow agents” break here because fixed scripts do not adapt well to long, multi step jobs.

DeepAnalyze fixes that with 5 actions, Analyze, Understand, Code, Execute, and Answer, so the model can switch between thinking and doing.

Training happens in 2 stages, first single skills are strengthened, then multi skill reinforcement in live environments. 

They also synthesize step by step trajectories so the model sees full examples of planning, coding, and using feedback.

Rewards are hybrid, simple checks like correctness and format plus an LLM judge that scores report usefulness and clarity.

The result is autonomous orchestration, choosing the next best action, and adaptive optimization, improving decisions from environment feedback.

Across many benchmarks, this 8B model beats most workflow agents and can produce analyst grade research from raw structured data. 

---

Paper – arxiv. org/abs/2510.16872

Paper Title: "DeepAnalyze: Agentic Large Language Models for Autonomous Data Science"

The most interesting part for me is where @karpathy  describes why LLMs aren't able to learn like humans.

As you would expect, he comes up with a wonderfully evocative phrase to describe RL: “sucking supervision bits through a straw.”

A single end reward gets broadcast across every token in a successful trajectory, upweighting even wrong or irrelevant turns that lead to the right answer.

> “Humans don't use reinforcement learning, as I've said before. I think they do something different. Reinforcement learning is a lot worse than the average person thinks. Reinforcement learning is terrible. It just so happens that everything that we had before is much worse.”

So what do humans do instead?

> “The book I’m reading is a set of prompts for me to do synthetic data generation. It's by manipulating that information that you actually gain that knowledge. We have no equivalent of that with LLMs; they don't really do that.”

> “I'd love to see during pretraining some kind of a stage where the model thinks through the material and tries to reconcile it with what it already knows. There's no equivalent of any of this. This is all research.”

Why can’t we just add this training to LLMs today?

> “There are very subtle, hard to understand reasons why it's not trivial. If I just give synthetic generation of the model thinking about a book, you look at it and you're like, 'This looks great. Why can't I train on it?' You could try, but the model will actually get much worse if you continue trying.”

> “Say we have a chapter of a book and I ask an LLM to think about it. It will give you something that looks very reasonable. But if I ask it 10 times, you'll notice that all of them are the same.”

> “You're not getting the richness and the diversity and the entropy from these models as you would get from humans. How do you get synthetic data generation to work despite the collapse and while maintaining the entropy? It is a research problem.”

How do humans get around model collapse?

>  “These analogies are surprisingly good. Humans collapse during the course of their lives. Children haven't overfit yet. They will say stuff that will shock you. Because they're not yet collapsed. But we [adults] are collapsed. We end up revisiting the same thoughts, we end up saying more and more of the same stuff, the learning rates go down, the collapse continues to get worse, and then everything deteriorates.”

In fact, there’s an interesting paper arguing that dreaming evolved to assist generalization, and resist overfitting to daily learning - look up The Overfitted Brain by @erikphoel.

I asked Karpathy: Isn’t it interesting that humans learn best at a part of their lives (childhood) whose actual details they completely forget, adults still learn really well but have terrible memory about the particulars of the things they read or watch, and LLMs can memorize arbitrary details about text that no human could but are currently pretty bad at generalization?

> “[Fallible human memory] is a feature, not a bug, because it forces you to only learn the generalizable components. LLMs are distracted by all the memory that they have of the pre-trained documents. That's why when I talk about the cognitive core, I actually want to remove the memory. I'd love to have them have less memory so that they have to look things up and they only maintain the algorithms for thought, and the idea of an experiment, and all this cognitive glue for acting.”

New APPLE paper says a small base model plus fetched memories can act like a bigger one. 

With about 10% extra fetched parameters, a 160M model matches models over 2x its size.

Packing all facts into fixed weights wastes memory and compute because each query needs very little.

So common knowledge and reasoning live in the base model, and rare facts live in memories fetched per input.

A retriever maps the input to a cluster path and fetches a small block from each level.

Those blocks plug into feed forward layers, the place transformers store facts, and this beats low rank adapters.

Only fetched blocks get gradients for related texts, which reinforces rare facts and avoids overwriting.

At inference the base stays in fast memory, and tiny blocks stream from slower storage as needed.

Teams can block, edit, or add memories to control what knowledge is available.

My brain broke when I read this paper.

A tiny 7 Million parameter model just beat DeepSeek-R1, Gemini 2.5 pro, and o3-mini at reasoning on both ARG-AGI 1 and ARC-AGI 2.

It's called Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) from Samsung.

How can a model 10,000x smaller be smarter?

Here's how it works:

1. Draft an Initial Answer: Unlike an LLM that writes word-by-word, TRM first generates a quick, complete "draft" of the solution. Think of this as its first rough guess.

2. Create a "Scratchpad": It then creates a separate space for its internal thoughts, a latent reasoning "scratchpad." This is where the real magic happens.

3. Intensely Self-Critique: The model enters an intense inner loop. It compares its draft answer to the original problem and refines its reasoning on the scratchpad over and over (6 times in a row), asking itself, "Does my logic hold up? Where are the errors?"

4. Revise the Answer: After this focused "thinking," it uses the improved logic from its scratchpad to create a brand new, much better draft of the final answer.

5. Repeat until Confident: The entire process, draft, think, revise, is repeated up to 16 times. Each cycle pushes the model closer to a correct, logically sound solution.

Why this matters:

Business Leaders: This is what algorithmic advantage looks like. While competitors are paying massive inference costs for brute-force scale, a smarter, more efficient model can deliver superior performance for a tiny fraction of the cost.

Researchers: This is a major validation for neuro-symbolic ideas. The model's ability to recursively "think" before "acting" demonstrates that architecture, not just scale, can be a primary driver of reasoning ability.

Practitioners: SOTA reasoning is no longer gated behind billion-dollar GPU clusters. This paper provides a highly efficient, parameter-light blueprint for building specialized reasoners that can run anywhere.

This isn't just scaling down; it's a completely different, more deliberate way of solving problems.

quote.text:
SpikingBrain’s technical report reveals a new family of brain-inspired LLMs. 

Learn how its hybrid-linear attention, conversion-based training, and spiking neurons deliver over 100x speedups and unprecedented efficiency on non-NVIDIA hardware.

100x faster first token at 4M tokens, with training on about 2% of the usual data. 

Transformers slow down as sequences grow, because each new token checks many earlier tokens and the memory cache keeps growing.

SpikingBrain mixes 2 cheaper attentions, linear keeps a small running summary, sliding-window reads only a short slice.

The 7B model alternates these layers for near linear cost, the 76B model adds parallel branches and a few full layers.

Feed forward blocks use Mixture of Experts, a router picks a small set per token so most weights stay idle.

The key idea is adaptive threshold spiking, activations become integer counts during training then expand into sparse events at inference.

A light conversion pipeline remaps a standard checkpoint, extends context to 128k, then finishes with supervised fine tuning.

Everything runs on MetaX C550 GPUs, the 7B model keeps memory near constant as inputs grow and accuracy stays close to baselines.

----

Paper Title: "SpikingBrain Technical Report: Spiking Brain-inspired Large Models"

since i got the engagement baiting version of this tweet out of my system, here's what this code actually does:

This is an implementation of a fallible mapping function try_map() for an array [T; N] where N=length

Try is a trait representing general fallibility or interruptibility, e.g. Option<U> or Result<U,E>

R is a type parameter that implements Try. So again e.g. Option<U>

F is a type parameter that implements a function that takes a T and produces a R. eg: T -> Option<U>, or concretely eg: String -> Option<usize>

Output is the associated type (the :: syntax) of Try that represents "success" or "normal execution", e.g for Option<U> it is U.

Residual is the associated type of Try that represents "failure" or "early exit" etc. In the case of Option<U> its Residual is Option<!>, where ! is basically Typescript's never type. Meaning: it is always None.

Residual is also a generic trait that lets you reconstruct the original Try type from its components. So if Option<!> implements Residual<U>, then its associated type TryType is just Option<U>.

So if we now look at the return type of try_map using our concrete example where T = String, F = String -> Option<usize>:

<Option<usize> as Try>>::Residual is Option<!>

<Option<usize> as Try>::Output is usize

<Option<!> as Residual<[usize; N]>>::TryType is Option<[usize; N]>

so:

you call try_map on an array of Strings [String; N] using a mapper function that takes each String and produces an Option<usize>, and the result you get is an Option<[usize; N]> - in other words, either you get a Some with all the strings mapped to integers or nothing at all.

The point of Try is that apart from F returning an Option, this also works for a F that returns a Result or any other Try type

I didn't go to college until I was 30. This gave me a chance to see it with the perspective of an adult. 

One lecture in Industrial Psychology, in particular, I will never forget. 

The professor spoke about how an effective job description focused on concretely measurable tasks, not vague instructions, or characteristics. 

For example, "maintain an 85% or greater average on customer feedback surveys", instead of "be cheerful and upbeat", or even "interact positively with customers".

This means that goals are clear, and performance is measurable. A job is to do something, not be something. 

Once some of the students had wrapped their minds around this concept, the professor decided to do a class exercise. 

He asked the female students to come up with a job description for "husband".  At first, this went fine. The girls noodled around a bit with things they wanted their husbands to be (tall, etc), but he was able to gradually steer them towards describing what they wanted in terms of actions. 

But then he asked the male students to define a wife in the same way. 

And all the girls became upset. Some of them had full-on meltdowns. 

Every single thing that a male student wanted, or expected, from his hypothetical future wife was sexist, oppressive, old-fashioned, misogynistic, patriarchal, etc. 

They were literally screaming. Some of them in tears. 

And I realized something pretty quickly. It wasn't the actual, concrete responsibilities of the female role that they objected to. 

It was the idea of there being a female role at all, with any attached responsibilities. 

These women didn't want to be wives. They wanted to be pets. 

What's a pet? Well a pet is not a wife, or a friend. A pet is a creature of instinct, which you bring into your home because you like how it naturally behaves. 

You get a cat because you want to behave like a cat, and do things a cat naturally does, like play with string, and purr when you pet him. If he's smart, he'll adapt you somewhat, but he doesn't have responsibilities other than "be a cat". 

If you get a wife, you get a wife so she will do things for you, specific things that are the responsibilities of wife, like care for your home, bear and raise your children, cook nutritious meals so you don't have to eat processed slop, look after your emotional well-being, and so on. 

These girls didn't want to be held responsible for those things. As married women, they might have anticipated doing some of them, but some of the time. When they felt like it. 

The cat chases the string if and when it wants to, not because chasing the string is its job. 

These young millenial women didn't realize it, but they wanted to be pets. And that's what they were in their college relationships. They hung out with guys when they wanted to, had sex with them when they wanted to, broke up with them for someone new when they wanted to. 

Their relationships had no element of reciprocal responsibilities. They were perfectly at home with the idea of men having responsibilities to them, but they would repay those men if they chose, and how they chose, not how the men actually wanted. 

And as I've said twice already, someone you have responsibilities to, but who has none to you, is a pet, or a child. 

The reason that a significant portion of men want to invent sentient feminine robots so that they can marry them is because they want wives, and they have given up on the possibility of young women re-embracing the concept of sex roles and actually having to do something for someone else. 

Women didn't spontaneously became more selfish than previous generations, of course. They were the targets of a concerted psyop whose purpose was to convince them that female responsibilities were demeaning. It was tailored to their unique psychological vulnerabilities, and they swallowed it hook, line, and sinker. 

Who mounted that psyop, and why, is a conversation most of us aren't ready for yet. 

But our point for today is don't worry, young ladies. 

The robots aren't being brought in to replace you. 

Just to do the jobs you won't do.

so, the way NeoGen works is by pattern-matching on the domain of the function we want to search. for example, if we're looking for a `ℕ → ℕ → ℕ` function, there are infinite ways to pattern-match the input:

λa. λb. match a { 0: _ 1+ap: _ }
λa. λb. match b { 0: _ 1+bp: _ }
λa. λb. match a { 0: match b { ... } 1+bp: _ }
λa. λb. match a { 0: _ 1+ap: match b { ... } }
... and so on ..

in NeoGen, we exhaustively enumerate all these pattern-matching shapes, *before* invoking HVM's superposed evaluator.

now, I was thinking about what are the actual "fundamental building blocks" of an algorithm, and this incomplete idea keeps occurring: there are multiple ways to split a set, and that matters. so, why are we sticking to just one? for example, the set ℕ can be split as zero/succ:

match n:
  case 0: ... // base
  case 1+p: ... // step

but it can also be split as even/odd instead:

match n:
  case 0: ... // even base
  case 1: ... // odd base
  case 0+2*p: ... // even step
  case 1+2*p: ... // odd step

and, indeed, many algorithms are much simpler in the later formulation. for example, `is_even`, with the zero/succ split, is:

def is_even(n: ℕ) -> Bool:
  match n:
    case 0:
      return True
    case 1+p:
      return not(is_even(p))

which is recursive, and uses an aux fn.

now, `is_even`, with the even/odd split, is just:
 
def is_even(n: ℕ) -> Bool:
  match n:
    case 0:
      return True
    case 1:
      return False
    case 0+2*p:
      return True
    case 1+2*p:
      return False

which is not recursive nor uses an auxiliary function. it is considerably simpler and easier to find.

now, here's the core intuition: isn't it the case that *all* functions can be expressed much more succinctly, given a suitable "special pattern-matcher"? for example, insert_sort can be expressed much more succinctly, given an eliminator that splits a list into "smaller element and rest":

def insert_sort(xs: [ℕ]) -> ℕ:
  match xs:
    case []:
      return []
    case min <: rest:
      return min :: sort(rest)

similarly, QuickSort can be easily expressed given an eliminator that splits a list into 2 chunks of values smaller/greater than a pivot element - and it also looks so much more elegant that way.  so, what if we enumerated all ways to split a set, instead of enumerating all functions constructed in a single specific way to split a set?

but how would that even work? as far as I know, no functional programming languages support that kind "special pattern-matcher", right? of course, we could just implement it manually with an aux fn, like:

// splits a list into (min, rest)
def split_min(xs: [ℕ]) -> Maybe (ℕ, [ℕ]):

and then just do:

def sort(xs: [ℕ]) -> ℕ:
  match split_min(xs):
    Nothing: ...
    Just (min, rest): ...

but, in the context of an enumerator, generating programs in that form is prohibitive, since we're pattern-matching on an unknown aux function, with an unknown type. this space is just immense. and even if it was possible, there's no guarantee that the generated function is actually splitting the set evenly. this just doesn't make sense at all

so, what captures this idea of "special pattern-matcher"?

I suppose that that what we want here is, perhaps, to find all types that are isomorphic to the input type that we have? for example, consider the type of Peano numbers, ℕ, and the type of bit-strings, 𝔹:

type ℕ ::= 0 | 1+ℕ 
type 𝔹 ::= 0 | 1 | 0+2*𝔹 | 1+2*𝔹

we know these types are isomorphic, because we can construct:

n2b : ℕ → 𝔹
b2n : 𝔹 → ℕ

such that `n2b . b2n = id` and `b2n . n2b = id`

so, what's on my mind is: if we had, in context, a type that is known to be isomorphic to the type we're enumerating, that would allow the enumerator to convert the input type to that isomorphic type, and then attempt pattern-matching on it instead:

def is_even(n: ℕ) -> Bool:
  match n2b(n):
    case 0: ...
    case 1: ...
    case 0+2*p: ... is_even(b2n(p)) ...
    case 1+2*p: ... is_even(b2n(p)) ...

here, pattern-matching on a function applied to an input argument (`n2b(n)`) is "justified" because of the isomorphism we have in the context.

but then, wait - if we're doing that, wouldn't it be more fruitful to, rather than enumerating "all algorithms", to, instead, enumerate all isomorphisms of the function's domain, and, then, attempt to find a direct functions for that new domain? as in - is_even and sort are trivial given the right isomorphism. I wonder if that's true for every algorithm we could find?

at least intuitively, it feels like finding the space of types isomorphic to the domain is much shorter, richer and more expressive than the space of all functions implemented as trees of pattern-matches - specially because such space is flooded with "garbage shapes" that are quite clearly not leading anywhere. see, for example, the image below, which enumerates all "pattern-matching shapes" of ℕ→ℕ→ℕ functions...

Pointer confusion in C is the result of the combination of a few grammar choices: 1) * being used for both pointer declaration and indirection 2) * having lower precedence than parentheses 3) function declarations containing parentheses that wrap parameters

Therefore declarations, especially those involving function pointers, can easily devolve into unparseable special character soup (K&R freely admit this and dedicate an entire section and exercise to it). 

Can you easily parse this declaration? What is x?: 

char (*(*x())[])()

Answer: x is a function returning a pointer to an array of pointers to functions returning char

(Source: K&R 2nd edition § 5.12)

Easy to dismiss head-scratching beginners with a simple "skill issue", but the actual authors of the language recognized how quickly readability can devolve in certain situations.

It’s the first time a lot of young men get feedback from the world around them that they are high in some form of status hierarchy.

We also know that motivation and success builds on itself. People who have no wins, ever, can sometimes just stop trying. Conversely, when people get the feedback that their effort produces results they want then they can become more agentic. A lot of young men haven’t had the opportunity to do much yet that would gain recognition from others. Imagine you want to find a function that inverts every 2 bits from a string:

```haskell
foo :: [Bit] -> [Bit]
```

For example:

```haskell
foo (0:0:0:0:0:1:[]) == 0:1:0:1:0:0:[]
```

As intelligent humans, we know the answer is:

```haskell
foo (x : 0 : xs) = x : 1 : foo xs
foo (x : 1 : xs) = x : 0 : foo xs
foo k            = k
```

So far, so good. But how do we find this function?

An enumerator with branching and recursion would try all possible "shapes":

Shape 1:
```haskell
foo (x : xs) = ... foo xs ...
foo []       = ...
```

Shape 2:
```haskell
foo (x : y : xs) = ... foo xs ...
foo (x : [])     = ...
foo []           = ...
```

Shape 3:
```haskell
foo (x : y : z : xs) = ... foo xs ...
foo (x : y : [])     = ...
foo (x : [])         = ...
foo []               = ...
```

The problem is that, in each of these shapes, recursion would diverge completely, making it inevitable to try all paths, causing a combinatorial explosion. But not only that, since x, y, z are bools, the enumerator could also match on them:

Shape 4:
```haskell
foo (0 : xs) = ... foo xs ...
foo (1 : xs) = ... foo xs ...
foo []       = ...
```

Shape 5:
```haskell
foo (0 : y : xs) = ... foo xs ...
foo (1 : y : xs) = ... foo xs ...
foo (x : [])     = ...
foo []           = ...
```

Shape 6:
```haskell
foo (x : 0 : xs) = ... foo xs ...
foo (x : 1 : xs) = ... foo xs ...
foo (x : [])     = ...
foo []           = ...
```

Shape 7:
```haskell
foo (0 : 0 : xs) = ... foo xs ...
foo (0 : 1 : xs) = ... foo xs ...
foo (1 : 0 : xs) = ... foo xs ...
foo (1 : 1 : xs) = ... foo xs ...
foo (x : [])     = ...
foo []           = ...
```

Shape 8:
```haskell
foo (0 : y : z : xs) = ... foo xs ...
foo (1 : y : z : xs) = ... foo xs ...
foo (x : y : [])     = ...
foo (x : [])         = ...
foo []               = ...
```

... and so on. There are many "shapes" to consider, and each shape forces a separate execution at runtime, breaking the superpositions of HVM...

However, notice the following: this same function, foo, can also be implemented differently—with only ONE pattern-match—if we introduce an auxiliary variable, b, and two non-recursive auxiliary functions:

```haskell
not : Bit -> Bit
not 0 = 1
not 1 = 0

bar : Bit -> Bit -> Bit
bar 0 x = x
bar 1 x = not x

foo : Bits -> Bit -> Bits
foo (x : xs) b = bar b x : foo xs (not b)
foo k b        = k
```

The idea is simple: the extra argument, b, alternates (0, 1, 0, 1...) at each call. When it is 1, we invert the bit; otherwise, we keep the same bit.

But what do we gain from this?

We gain that now the function foo has a single "shape":

```haskell
f : Bit -> S -> Bit
...

g : Bit -> S -> Bit
...

foo : Bits -> S -> Bits
foo (x : xs) s = f x s : foo xs (g x s)
foo []       s = []
```

In this case, the shape is: pattern-match once, emit one bit of information (f x s), and recurse, updating a state that is being propagated (g x s).

Every function from a stream of bits to another stream of bits can follow this same pattern, forcing multiple overlapping universes to always remain synchronized/convergent as recursion unfolds. Branching occurs only in the non-recursive functions, f and g, which is where the "search" happens.

There is a large cohort of both men and women who think that marriage is obsolete and that marriage will add no benefit to their lives or relationships.

It’s a diverse cohort, both ideologically and demographically. But at the end of the day you have people who think to themselves, “Why should I get married?” They don’t find any “arguments” in favor of marriage to be very convincing.

And some of the pro-marriage arguments are really terrible, to be honest. I say this as someone in the pro-marriage camp. The arguments aren’t bad because marriage is bad. In fact, on average marriage is associated with better relationships, longer relationships, more sex, more children, and is probably good for society.

The arguments are bad, because:

1. A minority of loud voices in the pro-marriage camp make marriage sound as awful as the “why should I get married” guys think it is. First comment I see when I open up responses to the post above is calling this guy’s girlfriend a name. Also things like: “Marriage isn’t supposed to be fun. Marriage is a terrible slog, but you do it anyway because it’s good for society and your duty.” This has convinced no one ever to get married! It is mostly just a talking point of resentful losers who are mad at women. The “marriage-as-authoritarian-fantasy” cohort will always be unappealing to everyone skeptical of marriage - and even the larger cohort of pro-marriage individuals who are able to form good relationships. 

2. No one abstains from marriage because of their “ultra-logical super-rational” self. Nor do they get married because of it. Basically you won’t argue people into getting married if they don’t want to. The decision to get married or abstain is based on a set of traits and dispositions that are a part of your personality. So, for example, if someone says, “Get married because married men have more sex,” no one who is married today actually thought to themselves, “I should get married because I want more sex. The sex I am having isn’t enough and I expect it to increase if I get married.” People get married because they have a traditional disposition, or romantic, or religious - which are all complex and heritable dispositions and traits.

If someone said to you “how do we get antisocial criminals in prison with a drug habit who love spending money at the strip club to be good husbands and role models” it might seem like an absurd population to focus on. If you have some familiarity with populations such as this, be it from a clinical or research perspective, or even personal experience, you might immediately know that they are not going to ever be that kind of person. It was simply never in the cards for them. 

But it isn’t just the extremes that are like this. A lifelong, happy marriage with no infidelity, abuse, etc. is not in the cards for many people either. The fast life history strategist - who fully expects that their relationship will not last forever (and due in large part to their own behavior and desires) - is making  pretty solid choice for himself or herself to not get married.

A big error people make is thinking that everyone is an interchangeable cog and that we can get everyone to behave similarly and that their outcomes will all be the same if we do. It simply isn’t so. The traits that make marriage work for you, or that make you value marriage and commitment in the first place, are not held by everyone in the population.

My take from GPT-4.5 is that humanity has designed an AGI architecture - it is just prohibitively expensive. This model is not great, because training a $1 billion transformer only gives us a 12.5% improvement over a $100 million one, in a paradigm where, apparently, utility scales logarithmically with training cost...

That also means that a dense GPT-5 would be only ~11% better than GPT-4.5, for the cost of $10 billion. Similarly, to get a jump as big as the one we've seen from GPT-2 to GPT-4, we'd need to train a GPT-7 (*not* a GPT-6), and that would cost about $100 trillion, i.e., the world's entire GDP. So, that's the wall: we saturated humanity's capacity to scale. Or, to be more specific, we'd need 1,000,000x more compute than GPT-4, to see that sort of jump again.

Some argue that reasoning breaks this wall, but I feel like it only weakens it. If test-time compute laws hold, then, we'd need a GPT-4 scale model to "think for 100 million tokens per output token" to emulate a GPT-7. Except it would take days to produce each token. That's not viable. So, unless we make 1,000,000 clones of planet Earth, we could be stuck at roughly this capacity for several decades, and never see a jump as big as the one from GPT-2 to GPT-4 again.

Unless, of course, new ways to improve the efficiency of these systems are discovered. AGI has become an optimization problem. I, for one, suspect that GPTs are embarrassingly sub-optimal, and that these big matrix multiplications are merely emulating an underlying "learning algorithm" with a massive overhead.

Now, it isn't hard to see that, at this scale, a single attention (i.e., "neural dict") pass takes easily more than 1,000,000x the compute than a dict lookup. If that is true, it wouldn't be surprising if the first team to break the "matmul wall" would be able to train a model equivalent to GPT-4 for as little as $100. Of course, attention is doing much more than a dict lookup; but we don't know what it is doing that leads to reasoning capacities. And, once we figure that out, we may be able to have GPT-7 for the cost of GPT-4, and not for the world's entire GDP.

That said, this would require a complete redesign. Gradient descent and matmuls have to be replaced by something entirely different - and nobody knows what that would be. It took us decades to go from neural nets to transformers, so, it could take us a decade to figure this out. Or someone could be stuck with a rush of inspiration and it would happen overnight...

Anyway sorry if I got some napkin math wrong, and all the respect for OpenAI for this release. Publishing a result that isn't a complete success is great science. Now I just want to understand what transformers are emulating, and how we can do the same, for less. I have many ideas, and I have many experiments to run... I'll try not to disappear completely but excuse me if I do

text:
Do not start with fundamentals. This is an awful approach to learning. 

Start with so-called "advanced" topics and ask questions until every term/concept is understood. 

This is the correct, rigorous, scientific way to learn, because the advanced topics are embedded in larger, more convoluted, more abstracted constructs. This embedding is what gives the individual pieces their *meaning*. 

Foundational studies have removed this embedding, and present only the isolated, sterile pieces. They have no meaning. They have no context.

The notion that students will piece together fundamentals into some eventual synthesis down the road is absolutely incorrect. It is literally information-theoretically obtuse. 

Children don't learn language using pieces. They mumble *fully*. They are never not fully embracing the complexity. It is the juxtaposition between their naive attempts and the full picture that imbues their mind with learning. 

Prerequisites are the dumbest approach to learning. It is utterly indefensible using any scientific argument. The basics-to-advanced directionality is diametrically opposed to how information is encoded, comprehended and used.

Prerequisites are why most computer scientists and whiteboard exam-passers can't make software themselves; they can only be cogs in a company. It's why a Princeton math PhD can write the update rule for gradient descent but can't draw the actual process with circles and lines on a damn chalkboard (true story). 

Idiot level stuff because their learning was all basics to advanced. They never defined terms and concepts in an embedded fashion. It was all disconnected. Meaningless muscle memory with no understanding.

It does not work both ways. Only pieces that are seen inside the bigger picture are understood.

Do not start with fundamentals.

Your brain doesn't forget - it just loses the keys to unlock memories

This paper introduces key-value memory architecture that separates storage and retrieval representations in brain memory systems, optimizing for both fidelity and discriminability.

-----

🧠 Original Problem:

→ Traditional memory models rely on similarity-based retrieval, limiting their ability to optimize separately for storage and retrieval

→ Current models can't explain how memories persist for decades despite rare access or how forgotten memories can be recovered

-----

🔑 Solution in this Paper:

→ The paper proposes a key-value memory system where inputs are transformed into two distinct representations: keys for memory addresses and values for memory content

→ Keys optimize for discriminability in retrieval while values optimize for storage fidelity

→ The hippocampus acts as key storage, while neocortex serves as value storage

→ Memories are accessed by matching queries to keys, then retrieving values weighted by match strength

-----

💡 Key Insights:

→ Memory failures occur due to retrieval issues, not storage limitations

→ Information once stored is never permanently lost

→ The brain implements error correction through attractor dynamics

→ Hippocampal representations optimize for discrimination while neocortical ones optimize for semantic content

-----

📊 Results:

→ Model demonstrates recovery of "silent" memories without retraining

→ Achieves 99% accuracy on initial tasks and 95% on subsequent tasks

→ Shows graceful degradation instead of catastrophic forgetting

→ Outperforms flexible encoders trained to minimize reconstruction error

Because it doesn't scale: even rank-2 types become a pain in the ass, let alone general rank-n types, indexed types, dependent types, linear types etc. The point of a type system isn't to limit what you can write but to assist you in writing that and to ensure that it doesn't change accidentally during a refactoring.

If your type inference practicalities break half-way towards a moderately complex program, they're crap. Type inference is supposed to be as compositional as everything else in a programming language (Agda for example does type inference very well).

Just commit to spelling polymorphism out when there's one and you open yourself up to a much more expressive type system designed to help you instead of limiting what you can do. And it's good practice to spell out types at definition site anyway, because it makes things more readable and reduces the chance of an error not being caught during a refactoring.

And if you still want Hindley-Milner-style inference occasionally for some reason, that should be a reflection plugin, not hardcoded into the language.

There is this perception that the median woman is run through by “bad boys” up until age 20, but the most common relationship pattern is serial monogamy and looks something like this:

1. Age 18-21: Dating someone for 1-4 years.

2. Age 21-24: Dating someone else for 1-4 years.

3. Age 24-28: Dating someone else for 1-4 years.

There will be a lot of individual variation here. A lot of men and women will have gaps in between where they have no sexual partners at all for 1-2 years.

A sizable minority of people will have a hook-up or two, but not very many. A lot of people will date for shorter or longer periods of time.

The chart below shows the annual distribution of sexual partners for men and women. In this same dataset, about 90% of sexual partners were in a committed relationship.

The 20s of the median woman looks less like a “cock carousel” and more like a relay race: long stretches with one partner before a break-up and finding a new one. The same is true for men as well.

All of these talk, dark, and handsome Chads are doing this too, by the way. Handsome and tall men are more likely to be in committed relationships. A lot of hook-ups and promiscuity is occurring at the mid levels. The truly ugly may be excluded entirely, but the truly handsome are not much more likely to be pursuing promiscuous sexual strategies.

“Bad boys” are behaving a little differently from the caricature, too. We tend to imagine someone having sex with a new woman from Tinder or the club every night.

But these are also the men who form long term relationships that just don’t last. All of those “baby mommas” were products of failed LTRs; very few from hook-ups.

You can imagine all of the men getting divorced in their late 20s, too. These are men much more likely to be high in antisocial traits, like the Dark Triad. So are all of the men who have been cheated on and end relationships that way. Yep, the “bad boy” gets cheated on even more than the “nice guy.” People who cheat, who have criminal records, or antisocial “Dark” traits are more likely to select people like themselves as prospective long term partners - and so their relationships are more likely to end badly!

So by age 30 or 35 you have a mix of woman who are single, most of whom haven’t been especially promiscuous but who have simply had all of their time tied up in a handful of relationships. 

Attractive, but promiscuous, women aren’t getting rejected either. Half of men don’t even ever ask about “body count.” Men who have been promiscuous themselves care even less. Incidentally, male virgins care the most!

What prevents women from being picked at age 30-35? Probably not much beyond (1) being unattractive (remember, half of the male and female population is overweight and at by age 35 your dating pool is substantially smaller - all of the “good relationship havers” don’t stay single that long) and (2) their own selectivity; they aren’t that attracted to the men around them. Half of single women at this age are single by choice vs only 10-20% of single men being single by choice.

text: How LLMs work, explained with visuals: https://t.co/nnDWsqEpMp

These 94 lines of code are everything that is needed to train a neural network. Everything else is just efficiency.

This is my earlier project Micrograd. It implements a scalar-valued auto-grad engine. You start with some numbers at the leafs (usually the input data and the neural network parameters), build up a computational graph with operations like + and * that mix them, and the graph ends with a single value at the very end (the loss). You then go backwards through the graph applying chain rule at each node to calculate the gradients. The gradients tell you how to nudge your parameters to decrease the loss (and hence improve your network).

Sometimes when things get too complicated, I come back to this code and just breathe a little. But ok ok you also do have to know what the computational graph should be (e.g. MLP -> Transformer), what the loss function should be (e.g. autoregressive/diffusion), how to best use the gradients for a parameter update (e.g. SGD -> AdamW) etc etc. But it is the core of what is mostly happening.

The 1986 paper from Rumelhart, Hinton, Williams that popularized and used this algorithm (backpropagation) for training neural nets:

text:
a lot of companies are focused on making ai better at writing code

but this doesn't feel like the right bet to me - it feels too tied to today's version of the world

i haven't been able to find much clarity but here's the rough thought process i keep having

first i try to picture a radically different future

ironically to do that, you have to identify something that won't be different

so i take a single type of interaction i predict won't change - restaurants will exist and will still take reservations

now we can try imagining how this might look different

today there is some kind of software the restaurant has that manages their operations

this software exposes availability info to an aggregator like opentable which lets consumers book across many restaurants

opentable sometimes does integrations with things like google maps so you can book without really involving opentable at all

so let's look at how far we can compress this scenario using ai

at some point someone with great distribution will build the ability to book restaurants through an ai interface - that doesn't just mean text it could also involve a ui

this is totally possible today through a permissioned integration with opentable

but if ai can directly drive browsers, you effectively have a  permissionless api to anything exposed on the internet, no need to do a specific integration with openai

if this ends up being popular, eventually most of opentable's traffic is coming from ai - do they still even need a traditional frontend?

maybe they drop it and just let their api be accessed publicly which ai can drive even more precisely

but can we compress this even further?

what value is opentable bringing here - they did the 1000 integrations with restaurant operations software to expose a unified data model

but ai doesn't really need a unified data model, it can figure out how to normalize anything on the fly

so you could say any business like opentable that solves a longtail type problem has less value

maybe the consumer facing ai product can talk directly to all of the restaurant management software and cut out a middleman

the restaurant management software itself will change but i don't think it'll go away

but it might be critical to ensure the restaurant's data is accessible to ai

this is sort of like SEO but for the ai world

so what's the conclusion here?

we've always wanted common protocols and open apis for everything but the coordination/consensus effort was way too high

ai might solve that but not needing consensus - it can book a reservation no matter the underlying data model

it also potentially eliminates aggregators that are doing this work manually

in a world where there's effectively standardized apis for everything, i don't really see why bespoke frontends (like opentable's website) will continue to be important

i can see how a handful of frontends will exist that can tap into this giant network of data and can operate the whole world

so ai that replaces a frontend engineer (which is where a lot of the initial focus is) does not seem super useful to me if frontend itself becomes less important

there's a few more things you can infer from this thought process but this post is long enough already
